newsitem.title: USA: Beneath Clinton rhetoric, a complex budget picture.
newsitem.headline: Beneath Clinton rhetoric, a complex budget picture.

text.p: When President Clinton said the U.S. budget deficit would be $50 billion to $100 billion next year without the balanced-budget deal, he neglected to say it will be a few billion dollars worse due to the deal.
Clinton's omission during a news conference on Wednesday is hardly surprising given that he signed the agreement into law this week that aims to balance the budget by 2002.

But it hints at the public relations battles that may lie ahead despite the mutual congratulations that the Democrats and Republicans have indulged in since reaching the pact's rough outline in May and agreeing on its details last week.

Some budget experts suggest next year's deficit may be far smaller than the $50 billion to $100 billion Clinton cited if the economy remains robust, possibly weakening Congress' resolve to make the spending cuts laid out in the agreement.
The administration has yet to publish its own year-by-year estimates of the effect of the balanced-budget legislation and is unlikely to do so before the end of August at the earliest.

But according to the administration's figures, calculated from the roughly drawn budget agreement sealed on May 2, the deal would aggravate the deficit by $1.5 billion in fiscal 1998, which begins this Oct. 1.
In each year thereafter, it would shrink the deficit, by numbers ranging from $19.4 billion in fiscal 1999 to $106.3 billion in fiscal 2002.
Those figures, of course, do not reflect the final legislation enacted this week.
But one administration official said the new projections would "roughly hew" to the old ones, suggesting that the deficit would indeed swell slightly in fiscal 1998.

According to Brookings Institution budget analyst Robert Reischauer, the budget agreement may widen the deficit by as much as about $19 billion in fiscal 1998, shrink it by about $3.6 billion in 1999 and more significantly thereafter.
"We sin in 1998, but are (close to) a wash in 1999 and beyond that it's significant deficit reduction," he said.

Burson-Marstellar budget analyst Stan Collender estimates the deficit would be about $6 billion wider in 1998 because of the budget agreement and would shrink thereafter, contracting by about $15 billion in 1999 and by $103.5 billion in 2002.
Robert Greenstein, budget analyst at the liberal Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities, sees a $15 billion widening in the deficit next year as a result of the deal.

The key reason for the widening next year, analysts say, is that the deal calls for higher spending than otherwise would be the case because it raises the mandatory caps on discretionary spending, while its tax cuts kick in immediately.

Whatever the effect of the deal, analysts say the more interesting question is what the deficit itself will be next year, with some arguing that the economy's strong growth, if it continues, may shrink it further or even yield a surplus.

Clinton said on Tuesday that the administration now expects the fiscal 1997 budget deficit to contract to $37 billion, well below 1996's $107 billion and a far cry from the record $290 billion in 1992, the year before he took office.
The exact answer of where the deficit winds up in 1998 in large part hinges on what economic growth one projects.

"If we were to maintain an unemployment rate of 5 percent ... we'd have a deficit that would be probably be lower than $37 billion to $40 billion," said Reischauer. While noting that such a robust economy was unlikely, he added: "We could (still) be pleasantly surprised next year."
Collender took an even more optimistic view.

"Under my numbers, if revenues grow at 6.5 percent, which is the average of the last four years, we're going to get a budget surplus next year," he said, adding that he does not expect the administration to make such a rosy assumption.

"They may want to save some good news to the fall or when the president's budget comes out in January or February," he said. "Wouldn't it be nice if (instead of) a $50 billion deficit we had a balanced budget or a $20 billion surplus?"

The only hitch, he suggested, would be if an early surplus were to undermine the discipline needed to hold the deficit down later. "If there's a surplus, there's going to be a lot of pressure to break the (mandatory spending) caps," he said.

Robert Brusca, chief economist with Nikko Securities Co. in New York, said he thought there was a "good chance" the budget may be close to balance next year. But he added: "Keeping your guard up during these times is going to be very difficult."
